43.title: Three strangers at the tent (Genesis 18:1–8)
43.hook: Abraham, still healing, runs in the heat to welcome three travelers
43.howItsDone: Jewish tradition counts welcoming guests as a mitzvah, a commandment: inviting travelers, students and people alone to a Shabbat or holiday meal is a common way it's done.

segments.voice: Last week ended with El Roi, Hagar's name for the God who sees. A new week begins at a tent door.

By now Abram has a new name: Abraham. He's ninety-nine, and he has just been circumcised, as the sign of God's covenant. He's healing. In the old JPS translation, the scene opens like this: "And the LORD appeared unto him by the terebinths of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day." The heat of the day: the hour when sensible people stay put. An old man sits in the shade of his doorway, sore. He looks up and sees three men standing near him. It's the doorbell ringing at the worst possible moment. And Abraham doesn't just get up. He runs.
screen: `NINETY-NINE, AND HEALING.` → `THE HEAT OF THE DAY.` → `THREE STRANGERS. HE RUNS.`

segments.voice: Hachnasat orchim. Literally, bringing in the guests: the Hebrew name for hospitality, and the rabbis point to this scene as its model. Watch the verbs. He runs to meet them. He bows. He hurries into the tent to Sarah: quick, three measures of fine flour, make cakes. He runs to the herd for a tender calf. The servant hurries to prepare it. For an old man, still healing, in the heat, that's a lot of running. And listen to what he promises: just a little water to wash your feet, rest under the tree, and "a morsel of bread." Then he serves fresh cakes, a whole calf, curds and milk. The sage Shammai taught, say little and do much, and the Talmud points to Abraham here as the example. The rabbis also asked: what was God doing there? The chapter opens with God appearing, and then Abraham turns away to the strangers. The Talmud reads it as God visiting the sick, coming to Abraham as he healed. And it draws a startling lesson: when the travelers came, Abraham asked God to wait. So, the Talmud says, welcoming guests is greater even than receiving the Divine Presence. There's also a tradition that Abraham's tent was open on all four sides, so a traveler from any direction would find a door. Nobody had to knock. The guests, the story later shows, were angels. But Abraham didn't know that when he ran. To him, they were just three tired strangers in the heat.
screen: `BRINGING IN THE GUESTS.` · `HE RUNS, HE HURRIES.` · `SAY LITTLE, DO MUCH.` · `GREATER THAN GOD'S PRESENCE.` · then, large: `A TENT OPEN ON FOUR SIDES.`

segments.voice: Think of the doorways in your life, your front door, your desk, your table, the empty seat next to you, and someone who might come through one today: a coworker, a delivery driver, a neighbor, a new kid at school, a relative. Picture offering them something small, a glass of water, a chair, a coffee, five minutes, quickly, before they have to ask. If you pray, you can ask for an open door.
Hachnasat orchim. Bringing in guests. Abraham's hospitality, running in the heat, and a mitzvah, a commandment, in Jewish life.
Your line: run to the guest. He promised bread and brought a feast. Until tomorrow.

44.title: Sarah laughs (Genesis 18:9–15)
44.hook: told she will bear a child at ninety, she laughs; the child will be Isaac, "he laughs"
44.howItsDone: Jews read Sarah's laughter in the Torah portion Vayera, and the rabbis' teaching that God changed her words for the sake of peace is often cited as a lesson about protecting peace at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was hachnasat orchim, bringing in the guests, and an old man running in the heat. Your line: run to the guest.

The three strangers have eaten. Then one of them asks a question guests don't usually ask: where is Sarah, your wife? In the tent, Abraham says. And the guest says: I'll come back this time next year, and Sarah your wife will have a son. Sarah is standing just inside the tent door, listening. She's about ninety. Abraham is nearly a hundred. The Torah says, with real frankness, that the time for her to bear children had long passed. So she does what anyone would do, hearing a stranger say something that absurd about their own body. She laughs. Not out loud. To herself.
screen: `WHERE IS SARAH?` → `A SON, THIS TIME NEXT YEAR.` → `SHE LAUGHS TO HERSELF.`

segments.voice: What she says inside is honest and a little funny: after I'm worn out, am I going to have pleasure, and my husband is old too? Then God speaks to Abraham: why did Sarah laugh, saying, shall I really bear a child, now that I'm old? Listen closely. Sarah said, my husband is old. God reports her as saying, I am old. The rabbis caught this, and loved it. The Talmud says God changed her words for the sake of peace in the home, so Abraham wouldn't be hurt. Great is peace, they said: even God shades a sentence to keep it. Then comes the question at the heart of the story: "Is any thing too hard for the LORD?" Sarah gets scared and denies it. I didn't laugh. The answer comes back, almost gently: "Nay; but thou didst laugh." Not a punishment. Just: you did. And it's not only Sarah. A chapter earlier, when God first promised this son, Abraham fell on his face and laughed too. Both parents laughed. So when the baby comes, a year later, Abraham gives him the name God had already chosen: Yitzchak, Isaac. It means he laughs, or he will laugh. The name keeps the joke forever. And Sarah, holding him, says: "God hath made laughter for me." Everyone who hears, she says, will laugh with me. Her laugh starts as disbelief and ends as joy, and it's the same laugh.
screen: `AM I, AT MY AGE?` · `GOD CHANGES HER WORDS FOR PEACE.` · `IS ANY THING TOO HARD?` · `YITZCHAK — HE LAUGHS.` · then, large: `GOD HATH MADE LAUGHTER FOR ME.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing that seems impossible to you right now: getting well, making up with someone, finishing the degree, changing a habit that's older than your kids. Say it to yourself plainly, and let yourself smile at it, even laugh a little, the way Sarah did behind the tent: not mocking, just honest that it seems absurd. Hold the laugh and the hope side by side, and if you pray, you can offer both.
Sarah laughs. Disbelief behind a tent door that turned into joy, and a son named Isaac, he laughs.

45.title: Father of many nations (Genesis 17:5)
45.hook: a convert asks if he may pray "God of our fathers"; the answer starts with Abraham's new name
45.howItsDone: Converts to Judaism traditionally take a Hebrew name as a child of Abraham and Sarah, and say every word of the prayers, including our God and God of our fathers. Who counts as Jewish by birth differs between movements.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sarah laughs, and a baby named he laughs. Your line: nothing is too hard. Today, step back one chapter.

More than eight hundred years ago, a man named Ovadiah sends a worried letter to Maimonides, the most famous rabbi of his day. Ovadiah became Jewish as an adult. Now his teacher has told him something that stings. When the prayers say our God and God of our fathers, Ovadiah should leave those words out. Abraham, Isaac and Jacob aren't his fathers. Can he say them or not? Maimonides writes back, and his answer starts in the chapter just before the three strangers came, when Abram gets a new name.
screen: `A WORRIED LETTER.` → `"NOT YOUR FATHERS."` → `MAIMONIDES WRITES BACK.`

segments.voice: On day forty-three, by the time the strangers came, Abram was already Abraham. Here's where it happened. God tells him, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Neither shall thy name any more be called Abram, but thy name shall be Abraham; for the father of a multitude of nations have I made thee." In Hebrew, av hamon goyim. Not the father of one family. The father of many. The rabbis of the Jerusalem Talmud used that verse to settle a question much like Ovadiah's: may a convert say our fathers? Yes, they said, because Abraham was made a father to everyone who comes in. Maimonides told Ovadiah the same, warmly and plainly. Say every word. Abraham is your father. Don't think less of where you come from. And remember the boy in the idol shop from day thirty-eight. In the story, the first Jew had no Jewish parents at all. So who counts as Jewish today? The movements answer in different ways. Orthodox and Conservative Judaism count a person born to a Jewish mother, or someone who converts. Reform and Reconstructionist Judaism also count the child of a Jewish father, when the child is raised Jewish. Conversions done in one movement aren't always accepted by another. Those differences are real, people feel them deeply, and this path won't pretend to settle them. On this path, there's no test at the door. One Jewish parent, two, or none. A partner, a convert, a grandchild who found a box of old photos, someone still unsure what they believe. Whatever brought you, there's a seat for you here.
screen: `ABRAM BECOMES ABRAHAM.` · `THE CONVERT SAYS "OUR FATHERS" TOO.` · `THE MOVEMENTS ANSWER DIFFERENTLY.` · `NO TEST AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Think back to whatever first pointed you toward this path: a parent or a grandparent, a partner, a friend's seder, a question you couldn't shake, a name on a family tree. Don't weigh whether it's a good enough reason; just let it come, and give it a moment of thanks. If you pray, you can thank God for the road; if not, notice that it led you here.
Ovadiah, the convert who asked Maimonides whether he could call Abraham his father, and was told to say every word: yes.
Your line: no test at the door. Whatever road brought you here, it counts. See you tomorrow.

46.title: Lot's wife looks back (Genesis 19)
46.hook: the cities fall, and a woman with no name turns to look
46.tomorrow: hagar and ishmael in the desert
46.howItsDone: Jews read the destruction of Sodom in the Torah portion Vayera; rabbinic tradition teaches that Sodom's sin was cruelty to strangers and the poor, and teachers often pair the story with Ezekiel's description of the city.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ovadiah, and Abraham made father of many nations. No test at the door. Now back to Sodom, which Abraham argued for on day eight.

Two of the travelers reach Sodom at evening. Lot is sitting at the city gate, and like his uncle, he jumps up, bows, and brings them home to eat. But that night the men of the city surround the house and demand the strangers be handed over. It's the opposite of Abraham's open tent: a city that turns on its guests. The visitors strike the mob blind and tell Lot: get your family out; this place is about to be destroyed. At dawn, Lot is still there. He lingered, the Torah says, dragging his feet. So the angels grab him, his wife and his two daughters by the hand, and pull them out. Run for your life, they say. Don't look back.
screen: `LOT WELCOMES THE STRANGERS.` → `A CITY TURNS ON ITS GUESTS.` → `DON'T LOOK BACK.`

segments.voice: Fire and sulfur rain down on Sodom and Gomorrah. Then, in the old JPS translation: "But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt." That's all we're told. She has no name in the Torah, and we never hear her say a word. Later tradition named her Edit, and the rabbis asked: why did she look? One old midrash answers with compassion. Some of her daughters were married and still in the city, and she turned to see whether they were following: a mother looking for her children. Another midrash, cited by Rashi, is sharper. When Lot brought the guests home, she wouldn't give them even salt for their food, and so she became salt. That ties her to the city's real sin, which in rabbinic tradition is cruelty. The prophet Ezekiel describes Sodom as proud and full of bread, living at ease, never helping the poor and needy. The Talmud tells stories of Sodom's laws against strangers and against charity. Maybe looking back means you can't be rescued from a place while your heart is still living there. Lot dragged his feet. His wife turned around. Read that way, the story doesn't mock her; it grieves. And near the Dead Sea today, on the salt cliffs of Mount Sodom, there's a pillar of rock that people call Lot's wife.
screen: `A PILLAR OF SALT.` · `NO NAME, NO WORDS.` · `LOOKING FOR HER DAUGHTERS?` · `SODOM'S SIN: CRUELTY.` · then, large: `SHE LOOKED BACK FROM BEHIND HIM.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you keep looking back at: an old argument you replay, a job you didn't get, a version of your life that ended. Looking back is human, and it can be love, like a mother looking for her daughters; but notice if it's keeping you frozen, thank it for what it was, then picture turning your face forward. If you pray, you can ask for help letting go.
Lot's wife looks back. A woman with no name, rescued by the hand, who turned toward the burning city and became a pillar of salt.
Your line: face forward. She was rescued by the hand, and still she turned. That's day forty-six.

47.title: Hagar and Ishmael in the desert (Genesis 21:9–21)
47.hook: sent away with bread and water, Hagar weeps; God hears the boy and opens her eyes to a well
47.howItsDone: Genesis 21, with Hagar and Ishmael in the desert, is the Torah reading in synagogues on the first day of Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish new year.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lot's wife looks back and becomes salt; your line was face forward.

Isaac is born, the laughing baby. When he's weaned, Abraham throws a great feast, and there Sarah sees Ishmael, Hagar's son, Isaac's older brother, laughing, or playing, or mocking: the Hebrew word shares a root with Isaac's name, and readers disagree about what it means here. Sarah tells Abraham: send this servant and her son away. Abraham is deeply upset, the Torah says, because of his son. God tells him to listen to Sarah, and promises that Ishmael, too, will become a nation. Early the next morning, Abraham takes bread and a skin of water, puts them on Hagar's shoulder, gives her the boy, and sends them away, into the wilderness of Beer-sheba.
screen: `A FEAST FOR ISAAC.` → `SEND THEM AWAY.` → `BREAD AND A SKIN OF WATER.`

segments.voice: The water runs out. Hagar puts her son under a bush, walks off about a bowshot away, and sits down. In the old JPS translation: "Let me not look upon the death of the child." She lifts up her voice and weeps. Then a detail with enormous weight: "God heard the voice of the lad." Hagar is the one weeping, but it's the boy God hears. His name, Ishmael, given by the angel before he was born, means God hears, and it comes true in the desert. An angel calls to her: "What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is." Where he is. The Talmud reads those words as God judging him as he is right now, a thirsty boy, not by anything that might come later. Then: "God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water." The verse doesn't say God made a well. It says God opened her eyes. The well was there all along; she was too deep in grief to see it. A midrash learns from this: all people are presumed blind until God opens their eyes. She fills the skin, gives the boy a drink, and the Torah adds: God was with the lad, and he grew. This chapter is the synagogue Torah reading on the first day of Rosh Hashanah, the new year. The year's reading includes a mother weeping in the desert, and a well she couldn't see.

48.title: The binding of Isaac (Genesis 22)
48.hook: the hardest story in Genesis; Jewish readers have argued over it for two thousand years
48.howItsDone: Jews read the Akedah on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, when the shofar, a ram's horn, recalls the ram; many prayer books also include it in the daily morning service.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Ishmael, God hears, and the well was there. Today's story is a hard one.

In the old JPS translation it begins: "God did prove Abraham." God calls his name, and Abraham answers with one Hebrew word, hineni: here I am. Then the command, each phrase heavier: "Take now thy son, thine only son, whom thou lovest, even Isaac." Take him to the land of Moriah, and offer him there on a mountain. This is the son Sarah laughed about: the son of the promise, the stars, the whole future. Abraham gets up early, saddles his donkey, splits the wood, and walks for three days. The Torah tells us nothing about what he feels. Jewish readers have argued over this story for a very long time; this lesson won't settle it.
screen: `GOD DID PROVE ABRAHAM.` → `HINENI — HERE I AM.` → `THINE ONLY SON, WHOM THOU LOVEST.`

segments.voice: On the third day, father and son walk up the mountain alone, Isaac carrying the wood. And Isaac speaks, the only time he does in this story: my father, he says, and then: "Behold the fire and the wood; but where is the lamb for a burnt-offering?" Abraham answers: "God will provide Himself the lamb for a burnt-offering, my son." And the Torah says: they went both of them together. Abraham builds the altar, binds Isaac, and lifts the knife. An angel calls: Abraham, Abraham. Hineni, again. "Lay not thy hand upon the lad." He sees a ram caught by its horns in a thicket, and offers it instead. Jews call this the Akedah, the binding, from the verb in the verse: Isaac was bound, not sacrificed. Here the tradition wrestles. Some read it as the peak of devotion, a man ready to give everything. It's read on Rosh Hashanah, and the Talmud connects the ram's horn, the shofar, to this ram. Others read the ending as the point: God stops the knife, and they hear the Torah saying no to child sacrifice. Others feel the silence. The same Abraham who argued with God for the strangers of Sodom says nothing for his own son. The next chapter opens with Sarah's death, and a midrash says she died when she heard what had happened. And when Abraham walks down the mountain, the verse mentions only him. Where is Isaac? The Torah doesn't say. None of these readings cancels the others. The tradition keeps them all, and keeps asking.

49.title: Sarah's burial (Genesis 23)
49.hook: Abraham buys the cave of Machpelah and pays in full to bury his wife with dignity
49.howItsDone: Jewish tradition buries the dead promptly and with dignity, begins with a eulogy and mourning, and remembers them each year on the anniversary, the yahrzeit, often by lighting a candle and saying the Kaddish.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Akedah, the binding, a story the tradition still wrestles with.

Sarah dies at a hundred and twenty-seven, in Hebron: the woman who left everything with Abraham, who laughed behind the tent flap, who held her impossible son. In the old JPS translation: "and Abraham came to mourn for Sarah, and to weep for her." Then comes a practical problem everyone who has lost someone knows. There's a body, and nowhere to put it. He's lived in this land for decades. God promised all of it to him and his children, and he doesn't own a single square foot. He gets up from beside his dead wife and goes to the local people, the children of Heth, to buy a grave.
screen: `A HUNDRED AND TWENTY-SEVEN.` → `TO MOURN AND TO WEEP.` → `NOWHERE TO BURY HER.`

segments.voice: Abraham introduces himself like every immigrant who ever stood in a government office: "I am a stranger and a sojourner with you." Sell me a burial place. The locals answer politely: you're a mighty prince among us; bury her in the best of our graves. Abraham wants one place: the cave of Machpelah, at the edge of a field owned by a man named Ephron. In front of everyone at the city gate, Ephron says: I give it to you. Free. Abraham says no, I'll pay. Ephron names a price, casually: four hundred shekels of silver, what is that between you and me? A lot, it turns out. Abraham weighs out the full amount, in the currency the merchants use, before witnesses. Why insist on paying? The commentators say: so no one could ever say the grave wasn't his. A gift can be taken back; a purchase stands. The quiet ache: the first piece of the promised land Abraham ever owns is a grave. Later, Abraham will be buried there, and Isaac and Rebekah, and Jacob and Leah. It still stands in Hebron today. Notice the order, too: to mourn, then to weep. The rabbis read the first as speaking about her, the eulogy, and the second as the tears. And in Torah scrolls, one letter in to weep for her is written small. Some say his tears were held in, even then. Grief deserved ground, and he paid in full.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who's gone: a grandparent, a parent, a friend, a teacher, even someone you never met but loved from a distance. Let their face come, remember one specific thing, a phrase they said, a dish they made, the way they laughed, and stay with it. You don't have to cry, and you don't have to hold it back; if you pray, you can hold them in your prayer.
Sarah's burial. The cave of Machpelah, bought in full. That's the seventh week: hospitality, Sarah's laugh, a father of many nations, Lot's wife, Hagar's well, the Akedah, and Sarah's burial.
Your line: grief deserves ground. Sarah rests in Machpelah, bought in full. Seven weeks, done.
